Club Meeting – North Museum of Nature and Science, 400 College Ave, Lancaster, PA 17603 Presented by Club President Andy McGann Andy McGann grew up birding in Southcentral Pennsylvania and his early experiences ultimately led to a career in the field of Movement Ecology. His time in academia, non-profits, consulting, and ultimately to a wildlife telemetry tech company spanned a timeframe that saw the science advance from analog radio telemetry to “smart devices” with GPS, accelerometers, and global Internet connectivity. In his career, Andy combined his experiences in ornithology with his love of technology and appreciation for geography in order to help wildlife researchers and organizations around the world obtain the scientific information needed to help conserve some of the rarest birds we have left. Surprisingly, virtually all of the youths return. But sometimes they don’t. Four out of the original six members of The Amish Outlaws were born and raised in Lancaster, PA and had a strict Amish upbringing. No electricity from land lines, no alcohol, no musical instruments, but their spirits were too wild for the Amish lifestyle. Once they trampled in the Devil’s Playground, there was no turning back. In the years since Rumspringa, the members of the Amish Outlaws have become very well acclimated to the pleasures and vices of the modern world… music, most of all. Hip hop, rock, country, metal, disco, opera. There is no genre they do not touch upon. Thus, with a bold lust for life and a fire for music and performance that can only come from 16 years of repression, The Amish Outlaws were unleashed upon the world. December 4–January 29 • Regitz Gallery Opening Reception: Friday, December 4, 2026 • 5–8 p.m. The Places We Go II is a solo exhibition by Ghanaian mixed-media artist Ross Junior Owusu exploring migration as an interior and ongoing process of becoming. Through ceramics, assemblage, and mixed-media artwork, Owusu examines how memory, resilience, cultural identity, and belonging are carried, reshaped, and rebuilt across shifting landscapes. Using fragmented materials such as clay and reclaimed objects, Owusu presents migration not as a fixed journey of loss or arrival, but as a layered negotiation of selfhood. His sculptural works reflect the physical and emotional imprints of movement, exploring what is carried forward, what is left behind, and what endures. Clay serves as a central material and metaphor in Owusu’s practice, reflecting cycles of becoming, un-becoming, and re-becoming. His sculptural forms draw from West African visual languages, including textured surfaces and modular interpretations of Krobo bead structures, while referencing architecture, the human body, and emotional landscapes. Reclaimed bicycle parts and earthy surface treatments further evoke movement, resilience, transformation, and connection to place. Through repetition, assemblage, texture, and vibrant surface treatments, The Places We Go II invites viewers to consider how identity is continually shaped and reshaped by movement, memory, place, and relationships. The exhibition features approximately 10 works exploring the complex connections between cultural heritage and evolving environments. About the Artist Ross Junior Owusu is a Ghanaian mixed-media artist and educator working across ceramics, performance, and assemblage. He holds an MFA in Studio Art with a concentration in Ceramics from Wayne State University and a BA in Industrial Art with a concentration in Ceramics from Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Ghana. He currently serves as an Assistant Professor of Art at Talladega College. Owusu’s artistic practice explores identity, migration, and cultural memory, examining how identities are carried, negotiated, and reassembled across changing geographies. His work combines contemporary mixed-media practices with West African visual languages, creating sculptural forms that connect inherited traditions with personal experience and contemporary environments.

Club Meeting – North Museum of Nature and Science, 400 College Ave, Lancaster, PA 17603 Presented by Peter Kaestner, legendary birder and retired diplomat Peter Kaestner relates his life-long quest to see 10,000 species of birds – a quest that was almost derailed on February, 2024, when another birder claimed the record just hours before Peter saw is last bird in the Philippines. Since then, Peter has maintained his quest, ultimately observing 10,000 species in the eBird and AviList taxonomies. Peter is a retired U.S. diplomat and an active independent birder who has spent a lifetime sharing his passion. On February 9, 2024, he achieved his ultimate goal when he saw his 10,000th species of bird, an Orange-tufted Spiderhunter in Mindanao, the Philippines on the IOC taxonomy. On October 21, 2025, he reached 10,000 on eBird, and on November 11, 2025, he recorded his 10,000th species on the new AviList harmonized world bird list. Always a birder, Peter took his first international trip at age ten, when he visited the Bahamas with his brother and mentor Hank. As of December 2025, he has birded in 196 eBird countries and territories. He is recognized by the Guinness Book of Records for having the world’s biggest life lists eBird (10022) and AviList (10,008) and as the first person to see a representative of every bird family – a feat that he accomplished in October, 1986. The highlight of Peter’s birding career came in 1989. Just 50 kilometers east of the Colombian capital, he discovered a bird new to science, the Cundinamarca Antpitta (Grallaria kaestneri). Peter graduated from Friends School Baltimore, where he received the William S. Pike science award and all-state honors in lacrosse. He studied Biology at Cornell University, graduating in 1976. Peter served in the Peace Corps in Zaire (Democratic Republic of Congo) as a secondary-school science teacher in 1976-1978 and joined the U.S. Department of State in June, 1980. During his 36-year career as a U.S. diplomat, he helped negotiate the UN Desertification Convention and a protocol amending the 1916 Migratory Bird Convention with Canada. He represented the United States at Conferences of the Parties of the Ramsar Convention and CITES. Peter has lived in 12 different countries: India, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, USA, Colombia, Malaysia, Namibia, Guatemala, Brazil, Egypt, Afghanistan, and Germany. Peter retired in 2016 from the State Department at the rank of Minister-Counselor. Peter loves sharing his passion for birds by writing articles, leading bird walks and tours, supporting local conservation efforts, and giving illustrated lectures on birds around the world. After the Colombian Government made peace with the FARC guerilla group, Peter helped it bring economic development to rural areas by promoting bird tourism. He also worked with the American Bird Conservancy and a Colombian NGO (Fundación Camaná) to preserve critical habitat of the Cundinamarca Antpitta in the east Andes. In 2019, Peter became a part-time tour leader for Rockjumper Birding Tours, in 2021 he became a VIP for Swarovski Optik, in 2023 he was appointed ambassador of the American Bird Conservancy, and in 2024 he received the American Birding Association’s Roger Tory Peterson Lifetime Achievement Award. Peter is married to Kimberly Vreeland Kaestner, and has two grown daughters, Laurel and Katie.

Working from a systems-thinking perspective, Yorty draws connections between a lifetime of experiences, passions, and joys to create opportunities for people to connect with themselves, one another, and their own stories through the process of making art together. Yorty’s artistic practice centers on participation, storytelling, and connection. Their work encourages people to own, tell, and participate in their own stories, reflecting a belief in art as a tool for personal expression, healing, and community.

October 2–30 • Regitz Gallery Opening Reception: Friday, October 2, 2026 • 5–8 p.m. Artist Talk: 6 p.m. Carolyn Harper’s Portrait Prison Project brings the lives and humanity of incarcerated and formerly incarcerated individuals into focus through hand-sewn, large-format quilts and hand-embroidered batiks. Many of the people Harper portrays are serving life-without-parole sentences in Pennsylvania, and many have spent decades behind bars. Harper does not seek to determine the innocence or guilt of the people she portrays. Instead, her textile portraits of incarcerated people focus on their individuality, dignity, humanity, and capacity for transformation. She has intentionally avoided asking the people she knows about the crimes that led to their incarceration, allowing them to share their stories on their own terms. Through these relationships, Harper has come to focus on redemption, rehabilitation, and the ways people change over the course of their lives. Every stitch is painstakingly sewn by hand, reflecting the minutes, days, and years that make up a life spent behind bars. The beauty and craftsmanship of the quilts and embroidered batiks create a striking tension with the difficult realities experienced by their subjects, inviting viewers to consider the humanity of people who are often overlooked or forgotten. About the Artist Carolyn Harper is a textile artist, educator, and advocate whose work combines portraiture, textile art, social justice, and activism. Raised in Rochester, New York, Harper moved to Philadelphia in 1989 to attend the University of Pennsylvania, where she earned an MFA studying under artists Neil Welliver and Rafael Ferrer. Harper has worked as an arts administrator and educator and has long been involved in volunteer and advocacy work. For many years, she created panels for the AIDS NAMES Memorial Quilt Project, taught art classes in homeless shelters, and advocated for homeless and incarcerated populations. She currently teaches classes and workshops in textile art, portraiture, and social justice art. Her current artistic practice brings together art, advocacy, and activism.

The Southeast Area tour highlights that liberation is up to African Americans, whose experiences represent a complex connection to their past—both the trauma of enslavement and the resilience of their heritage. This tour brings to life the triumph of the African American community as it built a culture of service, faith, and social activism, alongside the tragedy of Urban Renewal, which saw the demolition of 14 square blocks of thriving businesses, churches, and civic associations.
